The finding

Other models' translations can grade a formula

Can you tell whether an LLM's translation of a sentence is faithful when no gold formula exists?

Ask several independent model families to translate the same sentence, check with the solver which translations are logically equivalent, and score each candidate by the share of cross-family peers that disagree with it. That is the . A correct translation tends to have company; a wrong one tends to stand alone.

When the translators share a supplied predicate vocabulary (the condition), the score separates errors from correct translations almost perfectly on 221 long sentences with exception clauses, while a cheap LLM judge sits near chance. Under , the lead survives but shrinks by roughly 0.15 .

      How many cross-family peers does the score need before it stops improving?

      On development set E, the run drew k other families at random and scored each candidate against only those peers. Long sentences need more peers than short ones.

      Where it fails

      Long sentences, free vocabulary, renamed predicates

      Divergence grows with length when vocabulary is free

      Why does the free-vocabulary score weaken on the sentences where gold-free evaluation matters most?

      Split each population into word-length terciles and count the two ways a majority vote of peers goes wrong: errors the majority endorses (e) and correct translations the majority rejects (d). At a binary threshold the AUROC equals 1 − (e + d)/2.

      e: errors endorsedd: correct translations rejected

      The rename tradeoff

      What happens when a correct formula is rewritten without changing its meaning?

      Under free vocabulary the must match names across families. Rename the predicates of a correct formula and a name-based aligner loses its peers. The name-free variant c_nf is immune, but it cannot see errors that consist of a wrong predicate name.

      What the paper does not show

      • Confirmation is incomplete. Held-out confirmation was budget-stopped. On the one testable stratum of the fresh set (short ProverQA sentences), consensus ties a local Qwen-8B judge (Δ = +0.003 [−0.042, +0.052]); on 42 L25 items with 7 correct ones from 3 sentences it falls to 0.443.
      • Shared-signature scope. The 0.954 result uses templated sentences and a supplied vocabulary. It does not extend to translators that choose their own predicate names.
      • Development overlap. R_COMP-SIG later served as development data for aligner tuning, so the numbers on set E are not independent of it.
      • Provisional free-vocabulary labels. R_COMP FREE uses ERROR_CERT versus MAPPED, where MAPPED is an upper bound on correct; the labelling gate failed twice. The two-auditor subset gives Δ = +0.105 with a CI that barely excludes zero.
      • Label dependence. Set E labels come from a three-person panel with imperfect agreement; part of the advantage could reflect panel biases.
      • Cost. With nine peers the amortised consensus cost per candidate is about 19 times a single cheap judge call.
      • Error typing. Outside a shared vocabulary, typing the error is near chance: 0.123 accuracy on E, below the judge (0.326) and the peer-medoid baseline (0.328).
      • Domain. English to FOL only, from MALLS, ProverQA and R_COMP. Other formalisms and languages are untested.

        Glossary

        First-order logic (FOL)
        The target language of the translation: formulas with quantifiers (∀, ∃), predicates, connectives and negation. NL→FOL translation turns a natural-language sentence into such a formula.
        Z3
        The SMT solver used to check whether two formulas are logically equivalent. Equivalent formulas fall in the same class.
        Consensus score (c_score)
        c_score(c, s) = 1 − (1/k) Σ 1[equiv(c, pi)]: the share of the k cross-family peer translations of sentence s that are not equivalent to candidate c. Higher means more likely an error.
        Shared signature (SIG)
        All translators receive the same supplied predicate vocabulary, so equivalence is a direct Z3 check after case-insensitive symbol normalisation, and labels come from Z3 alone.
        Free vocabulary
        Each translator chooses its own predicate names, so comparing two formulas first needs a predicate-name aligner (c_score_align).
        AUROC
        The probability that a randomly chosen wrong translation receives a higher score than a randomly chosen correct one. 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect separation.
        Within-template / stratified AUROC
        AUROC that compares error and correct items only inside the same stratum (sentence template on R_COMP, source stratum on set E), removing confounds from stratum-level base rates.
        Disguised judge
        An LLM judge that reads the sentence and candidate with nonce predicate names, to control for memorisation of known benchmarks. The original-view judge sees the real names.
        Endorsement e
        The fraction of ERROR items endorsed by the peer majority: the false negatives of consensus.
        Divergence d
        The fraction of CORRECT items that diverge from the peer majority: the false positives (false alarms) of consensus.
        Predicate aligner
        Under free vocabulary, maps predicate names across formulas using structural cost, text-anchor cost and truth-value signatures, then declares a pair equivalent if any of the cheapest bijections gives a Z3-verified equivalence.
        R_COMP
        Long, complex templated sentences (at least 25 words, 4 to 5 conditions, with an exception clause) generated from a verified lexicon. Labels come from Z3 equivalence to references trusted by construction, one weak and one strong reading per template.
        Weak and strong reading
        The two accepted readings of an exception clause in R_COMP. For "A is B unless C" the weak reading is A ∧ ¬C → B; the strong reading is A → (B ↔ ¬C).
        Development set E
        8,507 candidate translations of 700 MALLS and ProverQA sentences. Its primary population R_AB, where both panellists agree, has 2,686 items (1,822 ERROR / 864 CORRECT, 292 sentences).
        Nonce and synonym renames
        Meaning-preserving rewrites of a correct formula: NONCE replaces predicate names with random nonsense names, SYN with WordNet synonyms. A metric should not change its verdict.
        False alarm (FA)
        A correct translation that the metric flags as an error.
